hops.title: The nail that went through the boot but missed the foot
hops.text: In 1995, a 29-year-old builder came into an emergency department after jumping down onto a 15-centimeter nail. It had gone through his work boot just behind the steel toecap. The smallest movement of the nail was painful, so doctors sedated him with fentanyl and midazolam before pulling it out from below. Then they took the boot off. The nail had passed between his toes, and his foot was entirely uninjured. His pain was real all the same. Pain and injury are not the same thing: the nervous system combines sensory input with context, and here the context was a nail sticking out of his own boot.

sources.citation: Fisher JP, Hassan DT, O'Connor N (1995) Minerva, BMJ 310:70; quoted verbatim in Hurwitz B (2017) Narrative constructs in modern clinical case reporting, Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 62:65-73 (PMC5471339)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A leather work boot with a long nail poking through the sole, beside a folded pair of clean wool socks on a wooden floor.
image.caption: The nail went between his toes and his foot was uninjured, yet his pain was real.

hops.afterHeading: What a line reports: the channels
hops.title: Vampire bats trim TRPV1 to sense warm prey
hops.text: Common vampire bats feed in the dark, and three pits around the nose help them find warm spots on warm-blooded prey. In 2011, Elena Gracheva, David Julius and colleagues showed that the bats did not need a new sensor for this. In the bat's trigeminal ganglia, alternative splicing makes a TRPV1 that is 62 amino acids shorter at its tail. Expressed in test cells, the short form opened at about 30 °C and the full-length form at about 40 °C. In the dorsal root ganglia the short form is under 3 percent of TRPV1 transcripts, so the body's nerves keep TRPV1 as a painful-heat detector.

sources.citation: Gracheva EO, Cordero-Morales JF, González-Carcacía JA, et al. (2011) Ganglion-specific splicing of TRPV1 underlies infrared sensation in vampire bats, Nature 476:88-91 (PMC3535012)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vampire bat on a wooden fence post at dusk, looking toward a cow asleep in a moonlit field.
image.caption: A shorter TRPV1, opening near 30 °C in test cells, helps vampire bat nose pits sense warm prey.

hops.afterHeading: Turning the report up and down
hops.title: Placebo pain relief is not just politeness
hops.text: It is tempting to treat placebo pain relief as politeness, or as talking yourself into ignoring an ache. In 1978, Levine, Gordon and Fields tested the question in people recovering from removal of impacted wisdom teeth. During recovery, patients got two doses an hour apart, double-blind. The reported analysis compared a placebo with naloxone, a drug that blocks opioid receptors. In patients whose pain fell or held steady after a placebo, a later dose of naloxone raised their pain, and their group's final average matched that of patients the placebo had not helped. The result suggests the body's own opioids helped produce the placebo relief.

sources.citation: Levine JD, Gordon NC, Fields HL (1978) The mechanism of placebo analgesia, The Lancet 2(8091):654-657 (PMID 80579)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A sunny wooden side table with a white capsule in a small dish, a paper cup of water and a chamomile flower in a small blue vase.
image.caption: After dental surgery, the opioid blocker naloxone undid placebo pain relief.
